subject: History of USA
title: 16. The Great Depression and New Deal

segments.text: The 1929 stock crash was a trigger and symptom, not the sole cause, of the Depression — judge the New Deal by three separate questions: did it relieve suffering, did it promote recovery, and did it permanently reform institutions?

Unequal income distribution, agricultural distress, consumer debt, speculative finance and fragile banks made the 1920s economy vulnerable well before 1929; the stock-market crash exposed these weaknesses rather than creating every part of the Depression by itself. Bank failures destroyed savings and reduced credit, while falling prices increased the real burden of debt, creating a destructive downward economic cycle.

The New Deal reduced suffering, stabilised banking, and permanently expanded federal responsibility, but unemployment remained high until wartime mobilisation — its greatest impact may be institutional and political as much as immediate economic recovery, a nuanced judgment worth stating explicitly rather than claiming full success or failure.

items.text: A memory framework for New Deal goals, useful only when attached to real programmes and outcomes rather than treated as a substitute for specific knowledge.
Use “Relief-Recovery-Reform” only as a memory framework, then attach real programmes and outcomes; explain the 1929 crash as trigger and symptom, not sole cause.
Do not say the stock crash alone caused the Depression.
Do not treat “Relief, Recovery, Reform” as a substitute for knowing actual programmes and outcomes.
Do not claim the New Deal fully ended unemployment before World War II.
The 1929 crash was followed by banking failures, deflation and mass unemployment.
Roosevelt took office in March 1933 and launched emergency banking measures; the Social Security Act (1935) established federal old-age benefits.
Full employment came only with wartime mobilisation, not the New Deal alone.
Judge the New Deal by three separate questions (relief, recovery, reform) rather than a single success/failure verdict.
The 1929 crash was a trigger exposing pre-existing structural weaknesses, not the Depression’s sole cause.
